title: Some say Ram, some Khuda
hook: some call Him Ram, some Khuda, some serve as Gusain, some as Allah (Ramkali M5, ang 885)

segments.voice: Yesterday, taatee vaao, the hot wind, and your line: in his refuge. Today, a shabad that walks through a whole street of neighbors.

Sunrise in an old Punjabi market town. From one direction, the call to prayer. From another, temple bells and someone chanting Ram. A man walks toward the river to bathe; another unrolls a mat to bow. Two neighbors greet each other in different words for the same morning. Guru Arjan lived in streets like that. And in one shabad he simply looked around and listed what he saw, without telling anyone they were wrong.
screen: `AN OLD MARKET TOWN AT SUNRISE.` → `BELLS, A CALL, A CHANT.` → `A SHABAD THAT LISTS WHAT IT SEES.`

segments.voice: The shabad is in Raag Ramkali, on Ang eight eighty-five. It opens, in paraphrase: some say Ram, Ram; some say Khuda. Some serve Gusain, some Allah. Ram is a name Hindus use for God; Khuda is the Persian word Muslims in India used. Gusain, a Lord, a master, was used by Hindu devotees; Allah, the Arabic name, by Muslims. Then the refrain: He is the Cause of causes, the Generous One; He showers mercy, the Merciful. Kareem and Raheem, generous and merciful, are Arabic names of God used in Islam, sung here in a Sikh scripture. The shabad keeps going down the street. Some bathe at holy rivers, some go on Hajj. Some do puja, some bow their heads in prayer. Some read the Vedas, some the Kateb, the books Muslims revere. Some wear blue, some white. Some call themselves Hindu, some Muslim. Some ask for one paradise, some for another. It's a portrait of a neighborhood, drawn fairly. Then the last line turns. Nanak says, whoever recognizes the Lord's hukam, the divine order, knows the Master's secret. The shabad doesn't say the names are all the same thing, or that the practices don't matter. It says that behind every name there's one Lord, and what counts is recognizing His will. It's a shabad for living alongside people who pray differently. In its view, a neighbor's word for God names the same One.
screen: `RAM, KHUDA, GUSAIN, ALLAH.` · `KAREEM AND RAHEEM IN THE REFRAIN.` · `A WHOLE STREET, DRAWN FAIRLY.` · `RECOGNIZE THE HUKAM.` · then, large: `MANY NAMES, ONE LORD.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind a name for God that isn't the one you grew up with, perhaps one a friend or neighbor uses, and say it silently once, with respect, the way you'd say a name you'd just learned. Then think of someone who prays with that name, and wish them well. If you pray, say Waheguru after it, and let the two names sit side by side.
Hukam, the divine order: Guru Arjan's shabad says some call the Lord Ram, some Khuda, some Gusain, some Allah, and the one who recognizes it knows His secret.
Your line: many names, one lord. A whole street of names, and one Master behind them. That's day six hundred sixty-eight.

howItsDone: Sikhs sing this shabad of Guru Arjan in kirtan, and often turn to it at interfaith gatherings as a picture of neighbors who name God differently.

fork.setup: the shabad has listed Ram, Khuda, Hajj, puja, the Vedas and more. where does Guru Arjan end?
options: by naming which practice is best.
by saying whoever recognizes the Lord's hukam knows His secret.
by asking everyone to stop praying.

original.note: Gurmukhi: some say Ram, Ram; the shabad's opening words, Ramkali M5, Ang 885.

trapdoor: what you thought: the shabad says all religions are the same.
what it means: it names many ways of praying fairly, and says one Lord stands behind them all.
what a scholar hears: the refrain uses Arabic divine names, kareem and raheem, and the close turns on hukam, a key idea of the Granth.

chat.says: Does Sikh scripture say anything about people who call God Allah or Ram?
options: Guru Arjan lists Ram, Khuda, Allah and more, and says behind every name is one Lord.
It says only Sikh names for God are right, and the others should be dropped.
It says all names and practices are the same, so none of them really matter.
chat.meaning: Guru Arjan's shabad lists Ram, Khuda, Gusain and Allah without calling anyone wrong; whoever recognizes the hukam knows the Master's secret.

Gusain.meaning: a Lord, a master; a name Hindu devotees used

Kareem.meaning: generous, an Arabic name of God

Raheem.meaning: merciful, an Arabic name of God

hukam.meaning: the divine order, the Lord's will

sources.ref: Ramkali Mahalla 5 (koee bolai raam raam koee khudaae), Ang 885

Glosses: Khuda as Persian, Gusain as 'a Lord, a master' used by Hindu devotees. Confirm.
